If the queue is empty the CPU idles until the next job arrives. A job enters the queue at its arrival time. When several things happen at the same time t, the order is: first every job that arrives at a time less than or equal to t and is not yet queued enters the queue (earlier arrival times first; jobs with the same arrival time enter in the order in which they appear in jobs), and only then the job that just used up its quantum at time t goes to the back of the queue. input.name: evalWithPositions
input.task: Evaluate an integer expression and return the value as a decimal string, or "ERR@p" when the expression has an error. p is the 1-based position of a character of text; every character counts, also spaces, tabs and line breaks, and the position text.length + 1 means the end of the text. Tokens: non-negative decimal integers (a run of digits is one token; leading zeros are allowed), the symbols + - * / % ^ ! ( ) and comma, names (a run of ASCII letters, a name is case-sensitive) and white space (space, tab, line feed, carriage return), which separates tokens and is ignored. Any other character is an error at its position. Grammar, from loosest to tightest binding. sum: product, then any number of "+" or "-" with a product, left to right. product: unary, then any number of "*", "/" or "%" with a unary, left to right. unary: "-" followed by a unary, or a power (so "--3" is 3 and "-2^2" is -4). power: a postfix, optionally followed by "^" and a unary (so "2^3^2" is 512 and "2^-1" has the exponent -1). postfix: an atom followed by any number of "!" (so "3!^2" is 36, "2^3!" is 64 and "-3!" is -6). atom: an integer; "(" sum ")"; or a name, "(", zero or more sums separated by commas, ")". Syntax errors. The text is read from left to right and the first token that cannot continue a valid expression is the error: p is the position of its first character, or text.length + 1 when the text ends too early (a missing operand, a missing ")"). Characters after the first error are never read, so a bad character that comes later does not matter. When a complete expression has been read, only white space may follow: any other token is an error at its position ("1 2" gives "ERR@3", "1)" gives "ERR@2", "1,2" gives "ERR@2"). A name must be followed by "(", white space allowed. An empty text gives "ERR@1". All syntax errors take priority over evaluation errors: nothing is evaluated unless the whole text is a valid expression. Evaluation. Integers have no size limit. Operations run in the order a left-to-right reading gives: the left operand first, then the right operand, then the operation; the arguments of a call run from left to right, and there is no short-circuit, so an argument is evaluated even when the call fails. The first error in this order is the result. "/" truncates toward zero and "%" is the remainder of that division, so it has the sign of the left operand (-7 % 3 is -1, 7 % -3 is 1). A zero divisor gives "ERR@p" with p at the operator. For "^" the exponent must be an integer from 0 to 200, otherwise the error is at the "^" (checked after both sides are evaluated); 0^0 is 1. For "!" the operand must be from 0 to 20, otherwise the error is at the "!" (0! is 1; "5!!" is an error at the second "!", as 5! is 120, which is above 20). Calls are checked after all their arguments are evaluated. The names are min and max (one or more arguments), abs (exactly one argument) and gcd (exactly two arguments, the greatest common divisor of their absolute values, gcd(0, 0) is 0). An unknown name or a wrong number of arguments is an error at the first character of the name. A result of zero is "0", never "-0".

edges.exponent-range: the exponent must be an integer from 0 to 200
edges.factorial-range: the operand must be from 0 to 20

You can start walking an edge at time t only if t mod period < open (1 <= open <= period; when open equals period the gate never closes). Once you have started, the walk always finishes after len time units. Waiting costs nothing: at any node, also at the start, you may wait any whole number of time units. You start at node from at time start (an integer, 0 or more). You also have one pass: on at most one edge of your walk you may ignore the gate and start walking at once. A generator makes a stream of integers: x(0) = seed and x(i) = (x(i-1) * 48271) mod 2147483647; the i-th number of the stream is x(i). Edge j (j from 0) takes the next five numbers a, b, c, d, e in this order: u = a mod n, v = b mod n, len = 1 + (c mod maxLen), period = 1 + (d mod maxPeriod) and open = 1 + (e mod period).

input.name: runRangeOps
input.task: An array a of integers starts with the given values and then receives a list of operations. All indexes are 0-based and inclusive. The operations are ["ADD", l, r, v] (add v to every element a[l..r]), ["SET", l, r, v] (set every element a[l..r] to v), ["SUM", l, r] (answer the sum of a[l..r]) and ["MAX", l, r] (answer the largest element of a[l..r]). Updates apply in order: a SET replaces whatever earlier ADDs did to those elements, and an ADD after a SET adds to the value that SET wrote. Before an operation is applied, l is raised to 0 if it is lower and r is lowered to n-1 if it is higher (n is the length of the array). A range with l > r after that step is empty: an update on an empty range changes nothing, SUM on it answers 0 and MAX on it answers null. Only SUM and MAX give answers; they are collected in the order of the operations. The array can be empty (n = 0): every range is then empty. Sizes and limits: n is at most 200000, there are at most 200000 operations, and every initial value and every v has an absolute value of at most 1000. Compact input. A generator with a seed s (1 to 2147483646) makes a stream of integers: x(0) = s and x(i) = (x(i-1) * 48271) mod 2147483647; the i-th number of the stream is x(i). values can be {n, seed} instead of an array: the array of n integers whose i-th element (i from 0) is the (i+1)-th stream number mod 2001, minus 1000. ops can be {count, seed} instead of an array: count operations, which need n of at least 1. Operation j takes the next four numbers of its own stream, p, l, r and v, in this order. Its kind is "ADD", "SET", "SUM" or "MAX" for p mod 4 equal to 0, 1, 2 or 3. With l0 = l mod n and r0 = r mod n its range is from min(l0, r0) to max(l0, r0). Its value is v mod 2001, minus 1000 (SUM and MAX do not use it). Return the object {count, first, digest}. count is the number of answers. first is the array of the first ten answers (all of them when there are fewer). digest summarises all answers: start with h = 0 and for each answer in order set h = (h * 1000003 + w) mod 998244353, where w is 0 for a null answer and otherwise w = ((answer mod 998244353) + 998244353) mod 998244353, plus 1.

edges.add-after-set: an ADD after a SET adds to the value that SET wrote
edges.clamp: l is raised to 0 if it is lower
edges.empty-range: A range with l > r after that step is empty
edges.no-answers: Only SUM and MAX give answers

input.name: onlineKth
input.task: values is an array of n integers with an absolute value of at most 1000000000 and a length from 0 to 200000. queries is an array of [l, r, k] with at most 200000 queries. The answer to a query is the k-th smallest of the values at the indexes l to r (0-based, both included), counting duplicates: k = 1 is the minimum and k = r - l + 1 is the maximum. In the values 4, 4, 4, 2, 2 the 2nd smallest is 2 and the 3rd smallest is 4. A query is invalid, and its answer is null, when l > r, l < 0, r >= n, k < 1 or k > r - l + 1. The queries of an array do not depend on each other. Compact input. A generator makes a stream of integers: x(0) = seed and x(i) = (x(i-1) * 48271) mod 2147483647; the i-th number of the stream is x(i). values can be {n, seed, maxV} instead of an array: the array of n integers whose i-th element (i from 0) is the (i+1)-th stream number mod (2 * maxV + 1), minus maxV. queries can be {count, seed} instead of an array, and then each query depends on the previous answer: last is 0 before the first query, and after a query it is that query's answer. Query j takes the next three numbers p, q and s of its own stream. With M(x, m) = ((x mod m) + m) mod m, set l0 = M(p + last, n) and r0 = M(q + last, n), then l = min(l0, r0), r = max(l0, r0) and k = 1 + M(s + last, r - l + 1). Compact queries need n of at least 1 and are always valid. Return the object {count, first, digest}. count is the number of answers. first is the array of the first ten answers (all of them when there are fewer). digest summarises all answers: start with h = 0 and for each answer in order set h = (h * 1000003 + w) mod 998244353, where w is 0 for a null answer and otherwise w = ((answer mod 998244353) + 998244353) mod 998244353, plus 1.

input.name: preemptiveSchedule
input.task: cpus identical CPUs (an integer of 1 or more) run jobs. jobs is an array of [id, arrival, burst, priority]: id is a unique string; arrival is the integer time when the job becomes ready (0 or more); burst is the integer CPU time the job needs (1 or more); priority is an integer, and a lower number is more urgent. jobs is not sorted. Time is whole and starts at 0. Rules. At every moment the CPUs run the most urgent jobs among those that have arrived and are not finished, at most one job per CPU. Jobs are ordered by priority number (lower first), then by earlier arrival, then by earlier position in jobs. A running job gets 1 unit of CPU time per time unit. A job that arrives at time t is considered at time t, so it can preempt a running job at t; a job that finishes at time t is not considered at t. A job that stops running while it still needs time is preempted; when it is chosen again it continues with the time that is left. Switching is free. A CPU with no job to run waits. Return one entry per job, in the order of jobs: [id, start, finish, preemptions]. start is the first time the job runs, finish is the time it completes and preemptions is the number of times it was preempted. An empty jobs array gives an empty array.

input.name: layoutText
input.signature: layoutText(text, width, justify) -> array of strings
input.task:
layoutText(text, width, justify) breaks a paragraph into lines of at most width characters and returns the array of lines (strings).

WORDS. Only the space character separates words. Leading, trailing and repeated spaces are ignored. Every other character, including tabs and line breaks, is part of a word and counts as one column. If the text has no words, return an empty array.

ITEMS. A hyphen "-" inside a word is a place where the word may be broken, but only when the characters just before and just after the hyphen are both letters or digits (A-Z, a-z, 0-9). So "well-known" can be broken after its hyphen, but "a--b", "-a", "a-", "x-(y" and "(a)-b" cannot. A break after such a hyphen leaves the hyphen at the end of the line, and the rest of the word starts the next line. The word is cut into fragments at these places, and each fragment ends with its hyphen (the last one has none). A fragment that is longer than width is cut further into pieces of exactly width characters (the last piece may be shorter); no hyphen is added there. The pieces of all fragments, in order, are the items of the word. Every item is at most width characters long.

LINES. A line is made of consecutive items of the text, from one or more words. Items of the same word are joined with no space between them; items of different words are separated by exactly one space. The length of a line is the number of characters it holds, spaces included, and it must be at most width. Every item must be on exactly one line, in order.

CHOICE OF LINES. Choose the lines that minimise the total cost. The cost of a line is (width - length)^2, where length is its natural length as defined above, except that the last line has no cost. If several choices have the same minimum cost, take the one whose first line is longest (the first line ends at the latest item); if that is still tied, the one whose second line is longest, and so on: the breaks are compared from the first line on, and the later break is better.

JUSTIFICATION. When justify is true, every line except the last is padded with spaces until its length is exactly width. The padding goes into the gaps, which are the places where two different words meet on that line (the spaces of the natural line). With g gaps and e = width - length extra spaces, every gap gets floor(e / g) extra spaces, and the leftmost (e mod g) gaps get one more. A line with no gap is left as it is, even when it is shorter than width. When justify is false, and for the last line, no padding is added. No line has trailing or leading spaces.

Return the lines in order. The text has at most 2000 characters and width is between 1 and 200.

input.name: binomialMod
input.task: Compute the binomial coefficient C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n-k)!) modulo m, and return the remainder as a number in the range 0..m-1. n and k are given as decimal strings, because n can be as large as 10^18, which a double cannot hold. 0 <= k <= n <= 10^18. m is a normal number with 1 <= m <= 10^9. m is not necessarily prime. Write m as a product of prime powers p^e, one for each prime p that divides m, where p^e divides m exactly. It is guaranteed that every such p^e is at most 2000000. Examples of valid m: 1000 = 2^3 * 5^3; 360 = 2^3 * 3^2 * 5; 1048576 * 953 = 2^20 * 953; any prime below 2000000. If m = 1 the result is 0. If k = 0 or k = n the result is 1 mod m. The result must be the exact value of C(n, k) mod m: when a prime power p^e divides C(n, k), the result is 0 modulo p^e, and when p^e is a proper power of p the usual theorem for a prime modulus is not enough on its own. The binomial coefficient itself can have far more than 10^17 digits, so it cannot be computed directly, and a loop that runs about min(k, n-k) times is too slow when that value is large.

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: The binomial coefficient modulo a prime power for n up to 10^18 needs the factorial-without-p technique, p-adic valuations, modular inverses, BigInt for the inputs and the Chinese remainder theorem. Plain Lucas is not enough for powers of primes. About 3 h for an expert who has not written it recently.

input.name: minPartitionCost
input.signature: minPartitionCost(n, k, maxA, zeroPct, fee, seed) -> number
input.task: A sequence a_1..a_n of non-negative integers is built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). For each i = 1..n, in order, draw two numbers: u = the next x, then v = the next x after it (two draws per element, 2n draws in total). Then a_i = 0 when (u mod 100) < zeroPct, and a_i = 1 + (v mod maxA) otherwise. Split the sequence into exactly k groups of consecutive elements; every group must contain at least one element, and every element belongs to exactly one group. The cost of one group is the square of the sum of its elements, plus the fixed fee. The cost of a split is the sum of the costs of its k groups. Return the smallest possible cost of a split into exactly k groups, as a number. Limits: 1 <= k <= n <= 16000; 1 <= maxA <= 200; 0 <= zeroPct <= 100; 0 <= fee <= 10^9; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. Every cost fits exactly in a double (below 2^53). When k = 1 the answer is the cost of the whole sequence as one group, and when k = n every element is its own group. Many elements can be zero, and then many different splits have the same cost. The inputs are far too large for a quadratic dynamic programme.

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Needs two techniques together: a Lagrange (Aliens) search over a per-group penalty, and a Li Chao or convex hull trick for each inner DP. Ties in the penalty search and exact integer arithmetic near 10^15 are the usual traps; about 3 h for an expert who knows both ideas.

input.name: runLumen
input.task:
Implement an interpreter for a small expression language called Lumen. runLumen(source) takes the program text and returns one string: the printed value of the program, or "error: <code>".

TOKENS. Spaces, tabs and line breaks separate tokens. A # starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. An integer literal is one or more decimal digits (leading zeros are allowed, so 007 is 7). A name starts with a lowercase letter a-z or an underscore, followed by lowercase letters, digits and underscores. The words let, rec, in, if, then, else, fn, true and false are keywords and cannot be names. The operator tokens are + - * / % ^ == != < <= > >= && || ! => ( ) , and = (the two-character tokens are read first). Any other character, including an uppercase letter, is a syntax error.

GRAMMAR, from the loosest binding to the tightest. An expression is one of: "let NAME = EXPR in EXPR"; "let rec NAME = FN in EXPR" where FN is a fn expression and the token right after "=" must be the keyword fn (so "let rec f = (fn x => x) in f" is a syntax error); "if EXPR then EXPR else EXPR"; "fn PARAMS => EXPR"; or an operator expression. PARAMS is a comma-separated list of names, and it may be empty ("fn => 1"). Two parameters with the same name are a syntax error. let, if and fn are only allowed where a whole EXPR is expected (the start of the program, after "in", "then", "else", "=>", "=", inside parentheses, and as an argument), so "1 + if true then 2 else 3" is a syntax error. The last expression of a let, if or fn extends as far to the right as possible.
Operator expressions, loosest first: (1) || ; (2) && ; (3) one comparison == != < <= > >= ; (4) + and - ; (5) * / % ; (6) prefix - and prefix ! ; (7) ^ ; (8) a call f(args) ; (9) an atom: an integer, true, false, a name, or an expression in parentheses.
|| and && and + - * / % are left associative: 10 - 3 - 2 is (10 - 3) - 2. A comparison does not chain: "1 < 2 < 3" is a syntax error. The right side of ^ is a prefix expression, so ^ is right associative: 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 is 2 ^ (3 ^ 2), and 2 ^ -1 is allowed. Prefix - and ! bind looser than ^, so -2 ^ 2 is -(2 ^ 2) = -4. A call has the form f(a, b); the argument list may be empty; calls chain, as in f(1)(2). The expression "!a == b" means (!a) == b.
The whole text must be exactly one expression. Empty text, a missing part, or any tokens left over are syntax errors. Every syntax error is found before anything is evaluated, so the program "1 / 0 +" gives "error: syntax".

VALUES. There are three kinds of values: integers, booleans and functions. Integers are exact (arbitrary size), but see overflow below. A function is a closure: it remembers the names visible where the fn expression was evaluated (lexical scope).

EVALUATION. Evaluation order is fixed, and the first error that happens ends the program.
- A name is looked up in the nearest enclosing scope; a name that is not found gives error unbound, and only when that name is actually evaluated.
- "let x = A in B" evaluates A in the outer scope (x is not visible in A), then evaluates B with x bound to the result. A new binding hides an older one of the same name. "let rec f = fn ... in B" makes f visible inside the fn body as well.
- "if C then A else B": C must be a boolean (otherwise error type); only the chosen branch is evaluated.
- A && B: evaluate A; it must be a boolean (otherwise error type). If it is false the result is false and B is not evaluated at all. Otherwise evaluate B; it must be a boolean (otherwise error type), and it is the result. A || B is the same with true and false exchanged. Operators are short-circuit.
- For + - * / % ^ < <= > >=: evaluate the left operand, then the right operand, then both must be integers (otherwise error type). For == and !=: evaluate both, then both must be integers or both must be booleans (otherwise error type; functions cannot be compared). Prefix - needs an integer and prefix ! needs a boolean (otherwise error type).
- / divides and rounds toward zero (-7 / 2 is -3); % gives the remainder that has the sign of the left operand (-7 % 3 is -1, 7 % -3 is 1). A zero right operand gives error div-zero (checked after the type check).
- a ^ b is a to the power b. A negative b gives error neg-exp. Any b gives a ^ 0 = 1 (including 0 ^ 0). For b > 0, 0 ^ b = 0, 1 ^ b = 1 and (-1) ^ b is 1 for even b and -1 for odd b, whatever the size of b. Every other base with b > 200 gives error overflow without computing the power.
- Overflow: whenever the result of a literal, +, -, * or ^ has an absolute value of 10^60 or more, the result is error overflow instead. (So 999...9 with 60 nines is a valid literal, and adding 1 to it gives error overflow; a literal of 10^60 gives error overflow when it is evaluated.) The checks of ^ come in this order: type, then neg-exp, then overflow.
- A call f(a1, ..., an): evaluate f first, then the arguments from left to right (all of them), and only then check, in this order: f must be a function (otherwise error type); the number of arguments must equal the number of parameters (otherwise error arity); the call depth must not exceed 200 (otherwise error depth). The depth of the program itself is 0, and the body of a function called from depth d is evaluated at depth d + 1. The call that would run at depth 201 gives error depth. There is no tail-call optimisation.

RESULT. The printed value of an integer is its decimal form with a leading - when negative; of a boolean it is true or false; of a function it is <fn>. The error codes are exactly: syntax, unbound, type, div-zero, neg-exp, overflow, arity, depth, printed as "error: " followed by the code.

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A tokenizer, a precedence parser with several special rules, and an evaluator with a fixed order of errors, over about 20 stated rules. The reference is about 270 lines. An expert needs about 2.5 h to read the rules closely, write it and chase the error-order and overflow corner cases.

input.name: offerChecksum
input.signature: offerChecksum(n, q, horizon, maxLen, xRange, seed) -> number
input.task: A shop lists n offers. Offer i is active during a time interval and sells at a price that is a linear function of the amount x: price = slope * x + base. A list of q price queries is asked. Everything is built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. Step 1: for each offer i = 0..n-1 in order, draw four numbers a, b, c, d and set start = a mod horizon, length = 1 + (b mod maxLen), end = min(horizon, start + length), slope = (c mod 2001) - 1000, base = d mod 1000000001. The offer is active at time t when start <= t and t < end. The end time itself is not included (a half-open interval). Slopes can be negative, so a price can be negative. Step 2: for each query j = 0..q-1 in order, draw two numbers a, b and set time = a mod horizon and amount = b mod (xRange + 1). The answer to a query is the smallest price slope * amount + base over all offers that are active at the query time. Several offers can be active at once, and many queries ask about the same time. When no offer is active at the query time, the answer is the number 4000000000 (no real price is that high). Fold the answers, in the order of the queries, into a checksum: h starts at 0; for each answer a, set h = (h * 1000003 + ((a mod 1000000007) + 1000000007) mod 1000000007) mod 1000000007, where a mod 1000000007 keeps the sign of a, as the % operator does in JavaScript. Return h as a number. Limits: 1 <= n, q <= 24000; 1 <= horizon <= 10^9; 1 <= maxLen <= 10^9; 0 <= xRange <= 10^6; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. All prices fit exactly in a double. The inputs are too large for checking every offer for every query.

edges.end-excluded: the end time itself is not included
edges.same-time: many queries ask about the same time

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Offline processing: a segment tree over time holds each offer on O(log q) nodes, and a Li Chao tree with rollback answers the minimum line at a point during a depth-first walk. Two data structures that must be combined with exact rollback; about 3.5 h for an expert.

input.name: countParses
input.task:
countParses(pattern, text) counts the ways in which a pattern matches a whole text. A way is a derivation: a complete record of which alternative was taken and how the text was split at every step. Two derivations that match the same text in different ways are counted as different.

PATTERN SYNTAX. A pattern is built from these parts. In a pattern, the characters | ( ) [ ] { } * + ? . and \ are special; every other character is an ordinary character that matches itself.
- alt: one or more sequences separated by |. Any sequence may be empty, so "a|", "(|a)" and "()" are valid.
- sequence: zero or more factors, one after the other. An empty sequence matches only the empty text.
- factor: an atom followed by zero or more quantifiers. Quantifiers stack: each applies to everything to its left in the factor, so "a+?" means (a+)? and "a{2}{3}" means (a{2}){3}. There are no lazy quantifiers.
- atom: an ordinary character; . (any one character); \ followed by any character c, which matches c itself; a group "(" alt ")"; or a class.
- class: "[" "]" around one or more items, with an optional ^ right after the "[" that negates the class. An item is a single character or a range lo-hi (lo and hi are single characters and lo <= hi by character code). A class matches exactly one character: one that is in some item (or, with ^, in no item). A - is a range sign when it sits between two characters; a - that is the first or last item is an ordinary character; any other - is invalid. A range uses both of its characters, so a - right after a range, as in [a-c-e], is invalid. \ escapes the next character inside a class, and an unescaped ] ends the class, so a class cannot be empty. ^ is only special right after the "[".
- quantifiers: * + ? and the counted forms {m}, {m,} and {m,n}, where m and n are decimal numbers (leading zeros allowed) with 0 <= m <= n <= 30.
If the pattern breaks any rule (an unmatched ( or ), a quantifier with nothing before it such as "*a" or "a|*", a } or ] on its own, a bad class, a bad counted form, a number above 30, m > n, a backslash at the end), the function returns -1. Check the whole pattern first: an invalid pattern returns -1 whatever the text is.

COUNTING. For a part X of the pattern and a piece s of the text, count(X, s) is the number of derivations of s from X. The whole result is count(pattern, text) for the whole text, so the match must cover the whole text. The rules are:
- an ordinary character, or \c: 1 if s is exactly that one character, else 0. For . and for a class: 1 if s is exactly one character that is accepted, else 0 (a class counts 1 however many of its items accept the character).
- a sequence x1 x2 ... xk: the number of ways to cut s into k consecutive pieces s1..sk (a piece may be empty) times the counts, that is the sum over all cuts of count(x1, s1) * ... * count(xk, sk). For k = 0 it is 1 if s is empty, else 0.
- an alt a1|a2|...: the sum of count(ai, s). Alternatives are counted separately even when they are equal, so "a|a" on "a" gives 2.
- a group: the count of its inner alt.
- X?: (1 if s is empty, else 0) + count(X, s). Taking X to match the empty string is a different derivation from skipping X, so "(a*)?" on the empty text gives 2.
- X*: zero iterations, or one or more iterations where every iteration matches a non-empty piece. So count(X*, s) = (1 if s is empty, else 0) + the sum over every non-empty prefix p of s of count(X, p) * count(X*, the rest of s). An iteration of a star must consume at least one character.
- X+: means X followed by X*, so count(X+, s) is the count of the sequence X X*. Here the first X may match the empty string.
- X{m,n}: the sum, over k from m to n, of the number of ways to cut s into k consecutive pieces (each may be empty) with a derivation of X for each piece; for k = 0 that is 1 if s is empty, else 0. The iterations of a counted repeat may be empty, unlike those of a star. X{m} is X{m,m}. X{m,} means X{m} followed by X*.

RESULT. Return the total modulo 67108859 (a prime), as a number in 0..67108858. Limits: the pattern has at most 80 characters and the text at most 60 characters. Intermediate products of two numbers below the modulus are below 2^52. Counts grow fast: "(a*)*" on 59 letters "a" has 2^58 derivations, and a brute-force enumeration of derivations is far too slow.

edges.star-nonempty: an iteration of a star must consume at least one character
edges.plus-def: x+: means x followed by x*
edges.rep-empty: the iterations of a counted repeat may be empty
edges.rep-open: x{m,} means x{m} followed by x*
edges.class: a class counts 1 however many of its items accept the character
edges.class-dash: a - that is the first or last item is an ordinary character
edges.whole-text: the match must cover the whole text
edges.invalid-first: an invalid pattern returns -1 whatever the text is

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A regex parser with class, escape and counted-repeat rules plus an interval DP that counts derivations with exact rules for empty iterations. About 25 rules to read and match; the reference is about 220 lines. An expert needs about 3 h, mostly to get the empty-iteration and stacking rules exactly right.

input.name: countValidPartitions
input.signature: countValidPartitions(n, k, d, cap, seed) -> number
input.task: There are n items numbered 0..n-1. Their weights come from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). For i = 0..n-1, in order, draw once and set weight(i) = x mod 1000. A weight of 0 is allowed. A group is a non-empty set of items. A group is valid when the sum of the weights of its items is a multiple of d, and the group has at most cap items. A partition splits all n items into groups so that every item is in exactly one group. The order of the groups does not matter, and the items are told apart by their numbers, so the partition {0,1},{2} differs from {0,2},{1}. Count the partitions into exactly k groups in which every group is valid. Return the count modulo 67108859 (a prime), as a number in the range 0..67108858. The count itself can be far larger than the modulus. If no such partition exists, return 0. Limits: 1 <= n <= 16; 1 <= k <= n; 1 <= d <= 12; 1 <= cap <= n; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. All intermediate products of two numbers below the modulus are below 2^52, so a double can hold them exactly. When d = 1 every group of at most cap items is valid. When k = n every item must be a group on its own, and when k = 1 the whole set must be one valid group. The number of partitions of 16 items is about 10^10, and a dynamic programme over all pairs of a set and its subsets is also too slow for the largest inputs.

edges.unordered: the order of the groups does not matter

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Counting set partitions into k valid groups for n up to 16 needs ranked (by group size) subset sums plus inclusion-exclusion over the union, and a truncated power of a polynomial per subset, all modulo a prime. A bitmask DP over submasks is too slow, so the expert has to know or derive the ranked transform; about 3 h.

input.name: countSharedSubstrings
input.signature: countSharedSubstrings(n, m, alphabet, seedA, seedB) -> number
input.task: Two strings A and B are built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. For a seed s, the generator draws x_0 = s and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). A string over an alphabet of size a (1 <= a <= 26; the letters are "a", "b", "c", ... in order) with length L and seed s has as its i-th character (i = 1..L) the letter with index (x_i mod a). A is built with length n and seed seedA. B is built with length m and seed seedB. Both use the same alphabet size. When the alphabet size is 1, every character of both strings is "a". Count the distinct non-empty strings w for which both of these hold: w occurs in A at least once, and w occurs in B at least twice. Occurrences may overlap: the string "aa" occurs twice in "aaa". A string that occurs many times is still counted once, because only distinct strings count. Return the count as a number (it can be larger than 2^32). Limits: 1 <= n, m <= 200000; 1 <= seedA, seedB <= 2147483646. The inputs are too large for any method that visits every pair of start and end positions.

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: The reference is about 60 lines: a suffix automaton with occurrence counts plus a second pass over the other string; an expert needs about 2.5 h to derive the counting rule, build it and debug the clone and count details.

input.name: evaluateSheet
input.task:
evaluateSheet(cells) computes a small spreadsheet. cells is an object that maps a cell id to the content of that cell, a string. Return an object with the same keys, in which every value is the text that the cell displays.

CELL IDS. A cell id is one capital letter A-Z followed by a row number from 1 to 99 without a leading zero, such as A1 or Z99. A cell id that is not a key of cells is a blank cell. The keys of cells are always valid ids.

CELL KINDS. The content of a cell decides its kind. (1) The empty string is a blank cell. (2) A string that starts with = is a formula; the text after the = is the formula. (3) A string made of an optional minus sign, then one or more digits, then optionally a point followed by one or more digits (for example 12, -3, 007, 2.50) is a number cell. (4) Any other string is a text cell and it displays as it is; so " 5", "1e3", "+4", ".5", "5." and "-" are text.

DISPLAY. A number is displayed as x.toFixed(6) with the trailing zeros after the decimal point removed, and the point removed too when no digit is left after it; a result "-0" is displayed as "0". So 2.50 displays as 2.5, 007 as 7, 1/3 as 0.333333 and 3.14159265 as 3.141593. A blank cell displays as the empty string. An error displays as its code. A text displays as it is. When the final value of a formula is blank, the cell holds the number 0 instead (so a formula =A1 with A1 blank displays 0).

FORMULA SYNTAX. Spaces and tabs between tokens are ignored. The tokens are: a number (digits, optionally a point and digits); a string in double quotes, where two double quotes inside stand for one quote character; a cell reference, which is one or more capital letters directly followed by one or more digits (A1, and also AB12, A100 and A0, which are not valid cell ids, see REFERENCES); a function name, which is one or more capital letters directly followed by ( ; and the symbols ( ) , : + - * / ^ & = <> <= >= < >. Anything else is a syntax error, including lowercase letters, and capital letters that are neither a reference nor a function name.
Operators from the loosest to the tightest: comparison (= <> < <= > >=), then &, then + and -, then * and /, then ^, then prefix minus. All binary operators are left associative, including ^: 2^3^2 is (2^3)^2 = 64. Prefix minus binds tighter than ^: -2^2 is (-2)^2 = 4, -2^-2 is (-2)^(-2) = 0.25, and 2^-1 is 0.5. An atom is a number, a string, a reference, a range (two references with : between them), a function call name(arg, arg, ...) with zero or more arguments, or an expression in parentheses. The whole formula must be exactly one expression; otherwise it is a syntax error, and the cell shows #ERR!.

VALUES AND ERRORS. A value is a number, a text, a blank, or an error. The error codes are #ERR! (syntax error), #REF!, #VALUE!, #DIV/0!, #NAME? and #CYCLE!. A reference to a cell whose value is an error gives that error. A reference gives: blank for a blank cell or a cell that is not in cells, the number of a number cell, the text of a text cell, the computed value of a formula cell.
REFERENCES. An invalid cell id (such as A0, A100, A01 or AB1) gives #REF! when the reference is evaluated, so it does nothing when it sits in a branch that is not evaluated.
RANGES. A range lists the cells of the rectangle between its two corners, whichever corner is written first, row by row (B2:A1 is the same as A1:B2; the order is A1, B1, A2, B2). If either corner is not a valid cell id, the range gives #REF!. A range gives #VALUE! when it is evaluated anywhere except as a direct argument of SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX or COUNT. A direct argument of IF, ROUND or ABS that is a range gives #VALUE! (this is checked before the number of arguments).

OPERATORS. To evaluate a binary operator, evaluate the left operand, then the right operand. If the left operand is an error, that error is the result and the right operand is not evaluated; otherwise if the right operand is an error, that error is the result.
- For + - * / ^ both operands become numbers: a number stays, a blank counts as 0, a text gives #VALUE!. Division by 0 gives #DIV/0!. A result of these operators (and of SUM and AVG) that is not a finite number, or that has an absolute value of 10^15 or more, gives #VALUE! instead; so 0^-1 and (-8)^0.5 give #VALUE!. Prefix minus needs a number or a blank (as 0), otherwise #VALUE!, and an error stays that error.
- & joins two texts: a number becomes its displayed text, a blank becomes the empty text, a text stays. The result is a text.
- = <> < <= > >= give the number 1 when true and 0 when false. If both operands are numbers or blanks, they are compared as numbers (a blank counts as 0). If both are texts, or one is a text and the other is a blank (the blank counts as the empty text), they are compared by character code, case-sensitive (so "A" < "a" and "10" < "9"). A text compared with a number gives #VALUE!.

FUNCTIONS. The functions are SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT, IF, ROUND and ABS. Any other name gives #NAME? and its arguments are not evaluated.
- SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT scan their arguments in order and collect numbers. For a range, the cells are scanned row by row: an error value ends the scan and is the result of the function; a number is collected; a blank or text is skipped. For any other argument, evaluate it: an error is the result of the function; a number is collected; a blank is collected as 0; a text gives #VALUE!. Then SUM adds the collected numbers (0 when there are none); AVG gives their sum divided by their count (#DIV/0! when there are none); MIN and MAX give the smallest and the largest (0 when there are none); COUNT gives how many were collected.
- IF(c, a, b) needs exactly 3 arguments, otherwise #VALUE!. Evaluate c: an error is the result; c must be a number or a blank (as 0), otherwise #VALUE!. If c is not 0 the result is the value of a, else the value of b. Only the chosen one of a and b is evaluated, so an error in the other one never shows.
- ROUND(x, d) needs exactly 2 arguments, otherwise #VALUE!. Evaluate x, then d; an error in x is the result, else an error in d. Then x and d must be numbers or blanks (as 0), otherwise #VALUE!, and d must be a whole number from 0 to 6, otherwise #VALUE!. The result is Math.sign(x) * Math.round(Math.abs(x) * 10 ** d) / 10 ** d, computed in double arithmetic.
- ABS(x) needs exactly 1 argument, otherwise #VALUE!. An error in x is the result; x must be a number or a blank (as 0), otherwise #VALUE!. The result is the absolute value.

CYCLES. A formula depends on every cell named in it: each valid reference, and every cell of each range whose corners are valid. This includes cells named in branches of IF that are not chosen and in the arguments of unknown functions, and cells that are not in cells. A formula with a syntax error depends on nothing. A cell is on a cycle when following dependencies from it leads back to it; a formula that names its own cell is on a cycle. Every cell that is on a cycle, and every cell that depends directly or indirectly on a cell on a cycle, shows #CYCLE! whatever its content is. This check is done first and overrides every other result.

SIZE. A sheet can have up to a few hundred cells and long chains of dependencies, for example 40 cells where each cell adds the next cell to itself twice (A1 is =A2+A2). The value of a cell must not be computed again for each use of it.

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A formula tokenizer and parser with unusual precedence (Excel-style ^ and minus), an evaluator with exact coercion, error-order and range rules, static cycle detection and memoised evaluation. About 40 stated rules; the reference is about 330 lines. An expert needs about 2.5 to 3 h to read, implement and debug it.

input.name: treePathChecksum
input.signature: treePathChecksum(n, q, window, bias, seed) -> number
input.task: A rooted tree with n vertices numbered 0..n-1 (vertex 0 is the root), integer values on the vertices, and a list of q operations are all built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. Step 1: for i = 1..n-1, draw r and set parent(i) = i - 1 - (r mod min(i, window)). So parent(i) < i. With window = 1 the tree is a single path 0-1-2-...-(n-1); a larger window gives a bushier tree. Step 2: for i = 0..n-1, draw r and set value(i) = (r mod 1000) - bias. Values can be negative. Step 3: for each of the q operations, draw four numbers r1, r2, r3, r4 in this order and set kind = r1 mod 3, u = r2 mod n, w = r3 mod n, d = (r4 mod 201) - 100. The vertices u and w may be the same vertex. The path between u and w is the unique shortest route of vertices in the tree, and it includes both endpoints and every vertex between them. If u = w the path is that one vertex. Kind 0 adds d to the value of every vertex on the path. Kind 1 is a query: its answer is the sum of the values on the path. Kind 2 is a query: its answer is the largest value on the path. The operations run in the order they were drawn, and a query sees all earlier additions. Answers can be negative. Fold the answers of the queries (kind 1 and kind 2 only, in order) into a checksum: h starts at 0; for each answer a, set h = (h * 1000003 + ((a mod 1000000007) + 1000000007) mod 1000000007) mod 1000000007, where a mod 1000000007 keeps the sign of a, as the % operator does in JavaScript. Return h as a number. Limits: 1 <= n, q <= 40000; 1 <= window <= n; 0 <= bias <= 1000; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. All sums stay below 2^53. The tree can be 40000 levels deep, so walking the path one vertex at a time is too slow, and a recursive depth-first search can overflow the stack.

edges.single-vertex: u and w may be the same vertex
edges.later-sees-earlier: a query sees all earlier additions

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Heavy-light decomposition with a lazy segment tree that keeps both sum and max, on trees up to depth 40000 (so no recursive DFS). The reference is about 110 lines; an expert needs about 2.5 h to write and debug it from scratch.
